It does not breathe oxygen. Along its flanks, folded gill-membranes extract dissolved hydrogen and simple nitrogen compounds from the sea and vent ammonia and methane. Metabolism is sluggish by Earth standards—chemical reactions run slowly in that cold—so the ammonite moves in long glides, coasting on stored chemical energy between rare meals.

Its outer skin is not lipid bilayer in the familiar sense. It is a tough, waxy sheath of ammonia-insoluble nitrogen polymers, studded with charged pores that let ammonia and small solutes through while holding larger organics inside. In the dim reddish light that reaches these depths, the sheath looks almost glass-clear, so the internal lattice of buoyancy bladders is visible: sacs of lighter hydrocarbons that it inflates or collapses to rise and sink without much swimming.

It feeds on “ammonia snow”—flocculent mats of carbon–nitrogen polymers that precipitate where warm seeps meet the cold ocean. A ventral siphon unrolls, lined with rows of needle-like rasps of silicon-nitride mineral. It does not chew so much as abrade and dissolve, drawing the slurry into a gut lined with enzymes that work in liquid ammonia and reassemble the fragments into its own polymers. Excess metal ions are sequased into glittering granules along the spine, which it later sheds as a glittering trail.

Senses are chemical and mechanical more than visual. A crown of stiff antennae tastes gradients of ammonia, hydrogen sulfide, and metal ions. Pressure organs along the ribs detect the slow heave of the sea and the footfalls of larger grazers. Reproduction is a quiet affair. In late “summer,” when the surface ice thins and the upper ocean warms by a few degrees, ammonites gather in loose schools above a seep. They release clouds of encapsulated spores—hard nitrogenous shells packed with a starter metabolism and a droplet of concentrated solvent. The spores sink, lodge in chemical-rich sediment, and over years grow into juveniles that look like pale commas crawling among the mats.

The ocean is clear in the shallows and tea-colored with dissolved organics farther down. Ammonia is less viscous than cold water would be at these temperatures in some regimes, but the whole world runs slow: metabolism is patient, and a “day” of feeding can last weeks.

### Body plan

It is about the size of a harbor seal, but flatter and more ribboned. The body is a translucent, slightly iridescent sac of pale gold, stiffened by a lattice of ammonia-insoluble polymers—think nitrogenous resins and long-chain hydrocarbons rather than calcium bone. It has no rigid skeleton. Internal pressure and a web of tense, cable-like fibers keep its shape.

Instead of gills or lungs, it has **solvent folds**: thin, frilled sheets inside a ventral chamber. Ammonia flows through them, carrying dissolved hydrogen, methane fragments, and simple nitrogen compounds. The folds are packed with catalytic membranes that pull energy from redox gradients—perhaps hydrogen reacting with oxidized carbon or sulfur compounds seeping from the seafloor. Oxygen is not the currency here. The atmosphere above is likely hydrogen- and nitrogen-rich, and free oxygen would be a poison or a rarity.

Its “blood” is ammonia itself, thickened with dissolved amides and carrying metal clusters (iron, nickel, maybe molybdenum) as electron shuttles. Circulation is slow peristalsis, not a pounding heart. A pulse might take minutes. Wounds clot with a sticky, waxy precipitate that hardens in the cold solvent.

Vision is poor. The eyes, if you can call them that, are shallow pigment cups tuned to the narrow band of light that penetrates ammonia and cloud. More important are **chemical combs** along the leading edges: rows of receptor hairs that taste gradients of ammonia, hydrogen sulfide, and organic amines the way a shark tastes blood. It also feels pressure waves through a lateral line of fluid-filled tubes, useful in a sea where sound travels differently than in water and where storms overhead can ring the whole water column.

It swims by undulating a trailing fringe, more kite than fish. When it wants to sink, it collapses internal gas bladders—small pockets of hydrogen or nitrogen—and folds its fronds. When it wants to rise toward a chemical plume, it unfurls and becomes a slow parachute. Top speed is a drift with intent. Chasing is rare; ambush and patience are the style.

### Feeding

It is not a hunter in the Earth sense. It is a **plume farmer and scraper**. Seafloor vents and cold seeps leak energy-rich molecules into the ammonia. Microbial mats—filmy, rubbery sheets of nitrogenous life—grow on those chemicals. The drift-lantern settles, everts a rasping skirt lined with silica-hard microteeth (silica and certain salts stay solid where water-ice chemistry would not), and shaves the mat. Some of what it eats is not digested so much as **fermented in place**: a gut that is more a warm pocket of catalysts than an acid bath. “Warm” here means a few degrees above the sea, maintained by slow exothermic reactions, insulated by a fatty, ammonia-repellent rind.

It also filter-feeds. When a current is right, it opens its fronds and lets dissolved organics adsorb onto sticky receptor films, then rolls those films inward like a tongue.

### Life cycle

Reproduction is seasonal in a way tied to orbital tilt or to pulses of nutrient upwelling, not to a warm spring. Adults bud. A lobe of the body wall thickens, loads itself with catalytic metals and a packet of genetic polymers—likely not DNA as we know it, but some other information-bearing chain stable in ammonia—and pinches off. The bud is a small, dense seed that sinks, rides a bottom current, and only unfurls when it tastes a seep.

There is no childhood sprint. A drift-lantern may take decades to reach full size and centuries to wear out, barring storms, ice falls from the surface, or larger scrapers that treat it as a mat. Aging looks like clouding of the sac and slowing of the catalytic metals as they leach away.

### What you would notice if you met one

It would not flee in a panic. It would taste you. A probe, a suit, a light—all of these are strange solutes and strange heat. The fronds might orient, the body might brighten faintly as internal reactions speed up near a warm object, and then, if you are not food and not a threat, it would simply resume its kite-drift, gold against black ammonia, slow as a thought in the cold.

None of this is a real species. It is a disciplined guess: life that uses ammonia as solvent must run cold, favor nitrogen-rich and hydrogen-rich chemistry over oxygen and water, grow slowly, and sense the world more by chemistry than by light. The drift-lantern is one way that guess could take a body.

A long, whip-thin tail carries electroreceptors. In ammonia, ions move readily; the skimmer reads the electric haze of swarms, storms, and the slow magnetic drift of the planet’s field.

Along both edges of the ribbon are rows of glassy filaments. They are not fins in the fish sense. Its sensory world is chemical and electrical. The head end is a blunt, slightly swollen bulb ringed with pits. They are sheets of folded tissue that trap thin films of ammonia and push them backward in coordinated waves. Its world is an ocean planet cold enough that ammonia stays liquid—far below the freezing point of water. Sunlight is weak and reddish. Ice floes of water and ammonia hydrates drift overhead like inverted mountains, and the depths are lit only by chemical glows and the creature’s own faint luminescence.

A vellid has no rigid skeleton. Its shape is held by a mesh of nitrogen-rich polymers, flexible at temperatures that would freeze Earth flesh solid. Embedded in that mesh are mineral grains—tiny crystals that act as ballast—so it can rise or sink by subtly changing how tightly it packs those grains.

Its “eyes” are not eyes. Along the leading edge are pits lined with pigments that respond to infrared and to the faint glow of dissolved compounds. It navigates more by chemistry than by sight: rows of sensory pores taste ammonia currents for dissolved metals, sulfur compounds, and the scent-trails of other vellids. Touch is continuous. The whole ribbon is a pressure organ, reading eddies the way a fish reads water, but slower, because the cold sea moves in thicker, lazier pulses.

### Chemistry of life

Where Earth life uses water as its solvent, the vellid’s cells are bags of liquid ammonia. Its membranes are not the familiar lipid bilayers of warm oceans. They are woven from molecules that stay fluid when ammonia would shatter ordinary fats—chains rich in nitrogen and short, flexible rings that do not crystallize in the cold.

Energy does not come from sunlight in any familiar way. Near the surface, some vellids host pigment patches that harvest the weak red light and drive slow reactions that split ammonia-compatible molecules, storing energy in nitrogen–hydrogen bonds. Deeper down, most of them abandon light entirely and feed on chemical gradients leaking from the seafloor: ammonia mixed with hydrogen, sulfur compounds, and metal ions welling up from warm vents that are still bitterly cold by human standards.

Metabolism is unhurried. A vellid’s “heartbeat” is a slow squeeze of internal ammonia sacs, circulating dissolved nutrients every few minutes rather than every second. Growth takes decades. A large adult may be older than a human civilization.

### Food and behavior

Vellids are not predators in the chasing sense. They are strainers and chemists. The frilled edges secrete a sticky, ammonia-stable mucus that traps tiny mineral flakes, microbial mats, and drifting organic grit. Special glands reduce those scraps into usable nitrogen compounds. When two vellids meet in a rich current, they often spiral together, sharing mucus films and effectively pooling their catch—less a hunt than a quiet merger of feeding surfaces.

They do have a defense. If a larger swimmer brushes them, glands along the ribbon release a burst of reactive nitrogen compounds that cloud the ammonia and burn the attacker’s sensory pits. The cloud is brief. In the cold, even “violent” chemistry is slow, so the vellid’s survival strategy is mostly to be uninteresting: pale, thin, and chemically quiet until touched.

Reproduction is a long, deliberate event. In certain seasons—marked by slight warming when the planet’s orbit brings a little more starlight—adults gather under the ice and extrude threads of genetic material packaged in tough ammonia-ice shells. Its “skin” is a membrane of long-chain amines and waxy hydrocarbons, impermeable enough to keep its internal fluid—a thicker, saltier ammonia solution—from mixing with the sea. The membrane beads rather than wets. Droplets of ocean roll off it the way water beads on a leaf, which matters: liquid ammonia has low surface tension, and anything that soaked it would lose heat and buoyancy at once.

It does not swim with fins. The mantle ripples in slow traveling waves, each crest lined with hair-fine cilia that beat in ammonia the way flagella beat in water, only slower. Instead of burning sugars in oxygen, it runs a nitrogen-cycle chemistry: it takes dissolved hydrogen and simple nitriles from upwelling plumes, and catalytic metal clusters in its tissues—iron, nickel, a little molybdenum—stitch them into energy-rich amines. Waste leaves as nitrogen gas in a faint trail of bubbles that never quite rise; they hang, silver seeds, until a current takes them.

Its eyes are not eyes. Along the leading edge of the mantle are pits filled with a clear, ammonia-stable oil. Temperature differences of a fraction of a degree bend that oil and tug on nerve-like fibers, so the animal “sees” warm chemical plumes and the cold shadows of other bodies. It also tastes the sea through pores that open only when a particular class of dissolved organics drifts past—markers left by its prey.

It has no voice and almost no social life. Once every long local year, when the haze thins and a weak sun warms the upper ocean by a degree, adults rise until their mantles nearly breach. They shed packets of genetic material into the ammonia—coiled, protein-wrapped strands that do not dissolve. Two packets that collide in the slow current fuse. Fine ammonia-stable filaments trail from its flanks like weed. They are not decoration. They are its lungs and its tongue.

Movement is a whole-body wave. There are no fins in the fish sense. The rear third of the body is a broad, rippling vane stiffened by mineral spars—ammonia-soluble salts would be useless, so the spars are built from silicate and metal-organic scaffolds the animal precipitates from the water. Thought, such as it is, happens across the whole surface. There is no single brain. A knot of denser tissue behind the leading edge coordinates the hunt, but memory and sensation are distributed. Injure one flank and the creature does not forget how to swim. It simply becomes less sure on that side, and relearns over weeks.

It senses the sea in three ways. First, chemistry: the filaments taste gradients of hydrogen, metal ions, and the faint nitrogenous trail of other ammonia-life. Second, pressure: the leading edge is a sheet of sensitive membrane that reads the push of distant movement, the way a jellyfish reads a current, only far more finely. Third, a weak electric sense. Ammonia is a poorer conductor than seawater, so electric fields fall off quickly; the kethral can feel another large body only when it is close. That is enough. In this ocean, close is where meals happen.

Its prey are not fish. They are colonial drifters—loose, balloon-like assemblages of smaller organisms that farm dissolved organics and rise and fall with the daily change in surface temperature. The kethral does not chase them so much as arrive inside their drift. It opens a ventral seam, not a mouth with jaws, and the seam’s lining is a field of microscopic hooks and solvent-stable adhesives. When the upper ocean cools further, hydrogen-rich layers sink, and the kethral rises to meet them. When the surface warms enough for ammonia to thin and boil into weather, it descends. Mating is a matter of chemical recognition and long contact. Two kethrals swim parallel for days, filaments interlaced, exchanging packets of genetic material that are not DNA but a related, nitrogen-heavy polymer stable in the solvent. There is no pregnancy in the Earth sense. The young hatch already able to taste hydrogen. They are the size of a hand, nearly transparent, and they do not school. The sea is too poor, and too slow, for crowds.

A kethral has no eyes that would mean anything to us. If you shone a lamp on one, the beam would scatter in the clear ammonia and the creature would feel the heat long before it understood the light—heat as a wrongness, a patch of membrane running too fast. It would turn away, not in fear exactly, but in the same reflex that makes it leave a rising warm layer. Its world is taste, pressure, and the long electrical hush of distance.

What you would remember, if you could stand in that sea without dying of the cold and the solvent, is not teeth or speed. It is the quiet. Its body is a single translucent sheet, scalloped at the edges, stiffened by ribs of a glassy nitrogen polymer that flex rather than break. There is no bone. Buoyancy is a problem in ammonia—the sea is light, and anything dense sinks—so the glasskite keeps most of its mass as a film. Inside the film, channels of slightly denser fluid run like veins in a leaf. They do not carry blood. Where the channels meet, pale knots glow faintly: clusters of metal-organic pigments, iron and nickel teased from the water, that catch what little red light filters down and turn it into a chemistry slow enough to live on.

It has no eyes in any familiar sense. Across the upper surface, thousands of clear lenses—really just thickened spots in the skin—focus blurry patches of light onto beds of those same pigments. The whole underside is a chemical tongue. Ammonia is a talkative solvent, and the creature reads plumes of dissolved metal, the sour trace of a decaying mat, the sweet alkaline wake of its own kind.

Food is a black snow. On the dim sea floor, and on the undersides of floating ice, mats of slower life pull energy from redox gradients—ammonia against dissolved oxidants seeping from the rock, or faint photochemistry where the ice is thin. They shed flakes. The glasskite drifts through these flurries with its margins rippling in a slow metachronal wave, each ripple timed to the low viscosity of the sea so that it sheds almost no turbulence. Flakes stick to a mucous film rich in hydrogen-bonding amides, then are drawn inward through temporary pores and dismantled. Nothing about this is quick. A meal can take a day. A digestion can take a week. The glasskite is not in a hurry; at these temperatures, almost nothing is.

When it must move with purpose—when a current threatens to fold it against an ice keel, or when another glasskite’s chemical wake grows too sharp—it vents a bubble of hydrogen from a small internal bladder and rises, or floods the bladder with dense brine and sinks. Steering is a matter of curling one margin and letting the ammonia peel away. It has no lungs and no gills in any Earth sense. Along both edges of the ribbon run rows of frilled siphons. They draw ammonia across catalytic mats that crack dissolved hydrogen compounds and simple nitrogen organics into usable energy. The reaction is slow. The brinewing is slow. It does not sprint; it unrolls.

Most of the time it rides the density layers where warmer ammonia from below meets colder ammonia from the ice-shelled surface. Its body is a single long muscle sheet braided around a flexible notochord of mineralized amide resin. A ripple starts at the head and dies at the tail, and the whole animal corkscrews forward with almost no wake. In ammonia, turbulence costs more than it pays. Stealth is the default.

The head is a blunt wedge with no eyes worth the name. Two deep pits, lined with chemoreceptive cilia, open and close like slow nostrils. They taste gradients of amines, cyanides, and the sour metallic signature of mineral seeps. Between the pits sits a pale organ, a living antenna: a strip of conductive tissue that senses the tiny charge differences other animals leave as they move. In Earth’s oceans that sense would be crude. Here, where the solvent is less forgiving of waste, even a small ion leak is a beacon.

Its mouth is not a jaw. It is a slit that everts into a soft, sticky proboscis lined with microscopic hooks of silicon-nitrogen glass. It does not bite prey so much as laminate onto it. Preferred food is not flesh in our sense but the drifting colonies of ammonia-algae—filament mats that photosynthesize poorly under a thick sky and instead fix energy from redox boundaries near the seafloor, then rise as buoyant skeins. The brinewing finds a skein, wraps once, and extrudes a digestive ammonia gel that loosens the mat into a slurry of amides and metal complexes. What it cannot use, it extrudes as pale, waxy pellets that sink and feed the vent gardens below.

Reproduction is a cold, careful affair. Once every long season, when the upper ice thins enough for a brief brightening, adults gather in slow gyres. They do not couple. Each sheds a capsule: a tough, amber bead filled with a concentrated non-aqueous yolk and a few embryonic ribbons already folded like watch springs. The capsules drift for years. Many freeze into the underside of the ice and wait through dim centuries until a warm plume frees them. A hatchling unspools already able to siphon. Childhood is just a smaller helix.

The brinewing is not alone, and it is not safe. Larger forms cruise the same layers: blind shear-eels whose bodies are almost pure conductive filament, stunning prey with sudden ion dumps; armored seep-crabs that mine metal crusts and will shear a brinewing in half if it drifts too close to a vent. Against them the brinewing has one dramatic trick. If grasped, it can vent a burst of supercooled ammonia from internal bladders, flash-freezing a shell of slush around the attacker’s grip, then tear free along a pre-weakened seam and regenerate the lost ribbon from stored amide reserves. ### Setting
Its ocean is liquid ammonia, roughly −70 to −40 °C, under a dense nitrogen–hydrogen atmosphere streaked with methane haze. Sunlight is weak and amber. The sea is less viscous than water and evaporates more readily, so waves are quick and fine, and shore ice of frozen ammonia and water-ice crusts the shallows. An adult is about two meters long and flat, like a manta crossed with a lily pad. Its body is a flexible lattice of nitrogen-rich polymers—chains closer to polyamides and nitrile-linked scaffolds than to Earth proteins—held in a gel that does not freeze solid at these temperatures. The “skin” is not a lipid bilayer of the water-world kind. Those membranes would dissolve or fail here. Instead it wears a woven sheath of fluorocarbon-like and long-chain nitrile sheets, beaded with charged ammonium groups that keep the interior chemistry partitioned from the sea.

Color is dull bronze and soot-black, tuned to absorb the little red light that reaches the surface and to shed heat slowly. Along the margins run translucent fringes, almost like kelp blades. They are not leaves. They are heat exchangers and chemical gills: thin sheets that let small molecules cross while the charged sheath holds larger solutes inside.

It has no bones. Internal pressure and a cartilage-like mesh of cross-linked amides keep its shape. Six radial “ribs” of stiffer polymer let it camber the body like a wing, so it can glide just under the surface or sink into slower, denser layers.

Energy does not come from breathing oxygen. Oxygen is scarce and, at these temperatures, a poor partner for its chemistry. The veil-skimmer runs on redox gradients already present in the ammonia sea: it oxidizes dissolved hydrogen and simple hydrocarbons against nitrogen-bearing oxidants—nitriles, hydrazine-like intermediates, metal amides leached from the crust. “Blood” is a circulating ammonia-amide solution carrying complexed metals—iron and nickel centers caged in nitrogen ligands—that shuttle electrons. There is no hemoglobin-red. Cut it, and the fluid is pale straw, smelling, if you could smell it without freezing, faintly of amines.

Eyes are useless in the haze below a few meters, so the eyes are small and only for the surface: two low domes that track the bright smear of the sun and the glitter of floating hydrocarbon films. Most of its world is felt chemically. It hears by pressure. A line of fluid-filled sacs along the ribs picks up the tick of distant ice calving and the thump of larger animals turning in the deep. Movement is a slow undulation. CREATURE DESCRIPTION:
The creature is a slow, cold-blooded swimmer built for an ocean that never warms above the temperature of a winter night on Earth. Call it a skimmer.

It is about the size of a small dolphin, but its body is flatter and more ribbon-like, with a broad, translucent hull of pale amber flesh. That color is not pigment so much as chemistry: its tissues are packed with ammonia-soluble lipids and nitrogen-rich polymers that stay flexible when water-based life would freeze solid. Its skin is not a waterproof barrier. It is a selective membrane, thick with a waxy outer cuticle that keeps the densest solutes in and lets liquid ammonia bathe a shallow network of pores. Through those pores it exchanges dissolved gases and small nitrogen compounds, the way a fish uses gills—except the “water” here is ammonia, and the useful chemistry is different.

Its metabolism runs on cold chemistry. Where an Earth animal burns sugars with oxygen, a skimmer’s cells use hydrogen-rich organics and dissolved nitrogen species, shuttling electrons through iron–sulfur and metal-organic complexes that work well below −40 °C. Reactions are slow. A heartbeat, if you can call the peristaltic squeeze of its vascular sacs that, comes once every few seconds. It does not sprint. It glides.

Propulsion comes from a pair of lateral fronds and a long, forked tail vane. The fronds are not muscle in the Earth sense; they are sheets of contractile fibers stiffened by a flexible mineral lattice, closer to cartilage than bone, because true bone would be brittle in this cold and poorly compatible with an ammonia solvent. The tail is edged with a fringe of sensory cilia. Each cilium is a hollow tube lined with ammonia-stable proteins that change shape when certain molecules bind. Taste and touch are almost the same sense for it. It “smells” the ocean by feeling which solutes stick.

It has no eyes that would work in sunlight. The sky, if it ever reaches the surface, is dim and the ocean is cloudy with suspended organic haze. Instead it carries a row of pressure pits along the snout and a chemical lantern: a gland that vents a faint plume of reactive compounds. Other skimmers taste that plume and answer with their own. Courtship is a slow chemical conversation carried on the current. A mating pair may circle for hours, matching plumes, before locking fronds and exchanging packets of genetic material suspended in a gel that does not dissolve in ammonia.

Food is whatever the cold ocean can offer. Near the surface, sunlight—if the star is close enough and the haze thin enough—supports a thin film of ammonia-tolerant photochemistry: amber mats of microbes that fix carbon and nitrogen into oily strands. Deeper, where the light fails, the skimmer follows chemical gradients leaking from the seafloor, grazing on microbial carpets and filtering drifting flakes of organic snow. Its mouth is a ventral slit lined with rasping ridges, not teeth. It does not chew. It abrades, dissolves, and absorbs.

Inside, the body is mostly solvent and soft organs. There is no blood of water and hemoglobin. A bluish circulatory fluid, rich in dissolved metals and ammonia-stable carriers, moves nutrients through open sinuses. Waste nitrogen is not a poison to be dumped; much of it is recycled. What it does excrete is a waxy pellet of carbon-rich residue that sinks and feeds the deep mats. Reproduction, growth, and even memory are paced to the cold: a skimmer may live for centuries, remembering chemical trails the way a salmon remembers a river, except the memory is written in stable molecular patterns rather than fast neural spikes. Its “brain” is a braided cord of slow fibers along the spine, good at holding long gradients and poor at split-second decisions it will never need.

It surfaces rarely. Liquid ammonia boils or freezes at the margins of its world depending on pressure and season, and the interface is a dangerous place—bright, chemically harsh, full of wind-driven spray. When a skimmer does rise, it is usually to cross a shelf or to lay a gel-packet in a sheltered lead. For a moment its hull catches the starlight, amber and almost glasslike, fronds trailing like torn sails. Then it folds, bleeds a trail of scent into the current, and sinks back into the slow black ocean it was built for.
